item.content:encoded:
I'm not sure why people were saying this doesn't seem anomalous. Losing understanding of the concept of quantities of things, and only losing that, is an incredibly specialized effect, much more than any existing virus has. Engineering such a virus is, at best, something humanity would not be able to accomplish for ages.

The SCP is a bit heavy on medical jargon at first and could probably benefit from being a bit simpler, especially where reader comprehension is preferred, like understanding what the rash looks like. That being said, the tone was set well and carried into the end of the article excellently, in my opinion. I was successfully scared.

I agree with the sentiment that civilization would cease to exist for anyone not immune to this. When every form of measurement is "as big as that other thing" because even the concept of being twice as big doesn't work, communication falls apart.

item.content:encoded:
I wanted to like this, particularly because of the accurate use of medical terminology; but couldn't. I'm just not seeing what is anomalous about this one. A virus that affects a particular part of the brain causing innumeracy is hardly anomalous, or even all that unusual. Aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia have all been noted as the aftereffects of viral infections or other brain trauma (though, typically, it's prenatal or early post-natal infection). The inability of someone with such a neurological deficit to recognize the deficit is also commonplace, Alzheimer's cases being an obvious case in point, but there are plenty of others.

Likewise, there are a number of viruses whose structure makes it effectively impossible, or at least extremely difficult, with current medical technology to develop anything like a functional vaccine. HIV and Herpes Simplex being the obvious examples here.

Had to vote this one down for lack of anything actually anomalous.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: Nah. Measles cross-immunity doesn't apply- as the last paragraph noted, outbreaks of measles in populations where measles vaccine uptake is normally high should be investigated for this. Given that this is an article for the Foundation, the possibility exists that someone who was exposed to SCP-593 morbillivirus might have been given either SCP-500 or a quick trip to that kid who absorbs your illness, and therefore a small immune population could conceivably exist. That's all.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
Can you imagine what would happen if this thing got out without a proper vaccine? With such a high infection rate, it might lead to the end of modern society! Imagine a world where nobody could count! So many things would fall apart that we'd be blasted back to the Stone Age. No ability to judge proportions, no ability to handle sets of objects…

Since the symptoms take time to develop, as well as being relatively hidden, lots of people would catch the virus before they knew of its effects. This might help the virus spread until quarantine becomes ineffective.

The article notes that ninety percent of non-immune people will contract the disease within thirty days; I'm not entirely sure where they would get their immunity from, given that the article also declares the standard measles vaccine ineffective. Does innate measles resistance also protect against SCP-593? If so, this gets a bit less scary.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: I'd also like it noted that victims of this particular disease aren't even bothered by their sudden total innumeracy. It is entirely possible that someone who recovers from the illness won't mention their lack of ability to tell the difference between 'four' and 'ninety' to anyone until it's too late.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: I had two alternative candidates for the initial release spot. One was going to be the Tokyo stock exchange trading floor, and the other was going to be Grand Central Station- but the latter's just a fairly generic terrorist attack site, not one particularly focused on the financial industry, so the NYSE won the deal.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
One, that it is so consistently targeted. There are plenty of real-world viruses that cause brain damage, yes. Measles itself can do so; there's an entire syndrome that attacks the brain of individuals who were infected before age two, years after the fact, and essentially turns their brain into Swiss cheese before killing them. But this virus very specifically targets one area of the brain and one only, which points directly to it being genetically engineered by whoever hitched it up to the stock exchange's trading floor.

Which leads to reason two: the amount of sheer havoc a virus that destroyed its victims' concept of number could do if released in the appropriate places. If ninety per cent of every single person on the trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange- or the Nikkei, or, hell, any air traffic control center-lost the ability to comprehend numbers, the amount of damage to the world economy would be, literally, incalculable. The Foundation gets involved because the last thing they want is the possibility of whoever created this damn thing popping up again and killing entire economies with a few well-timed cases of what looks like measles.
